links.note: Turning the speech bubbles of the three men, and then of the sepoys, into reported speech is 31568, the direct-to-indirect narration the comic form is used to teach. 31569 is the specific farmer-and-tax-officer exchange, which is a different set of bubbles.
Rewriting the farmers' speech bubbles as dialogue and playacting their grievance against the tax policy is 31569 exactly. 31568 is the general narration rule.

The fox-and-goat panels are worked through a sequence of who-and-where questions before the story is written - picture reading as a skill with steps, which is 31560's point. 31558 is about the comic conveying the history.
The news item is about teaching history through comic strips and visuals; 31558 is that claim - pictures and speech bubbles are what clarify the conditions leading to the revolt.
Asks the learner to notice that several history chapters are condensed into a few pages by pictures and speech bubbles - 31558's own wording.
Making a comic of the Sun and Wind fable applies the picture-plus-bubble form of 31558. 31568 is the narration grammar, which this task does not ask about.

Child marriage, untouchability and the inferiority of women are the practices the reform panels set Ram Mohan Roy against; this set holds that whole section only as 31565. 31563 is the jailing regulation, a different kind of oppression.
Duty-free entry for English goods is the mechanism behind the artisans' ruin that 31564 asks learners to explain. 31562 is military superiority, not trade policy.
Identifies Ram Mohan Roy as the man who fought superstition - the reformer 31565 is built on. Tipu (31561) is the distractor from the earlier panels.
The cows-of-different-colours line is Roy's own saying that every religion teaches the same principles - 31565 word for word.
The newspapers stopped in 1823 were Roy's, and this set carries his work only at 31565. 31563 is Regulation III, the other repressive measure in these panels.
The cotton weavers' misery is the artisan ruin of 31564. 31569 is the farmers' grievance, the parallel case.
'The bones of the cotton weavers are bleaching the plains of India' is the line that sums up 31564. The attribution is what the distractors test.
The whole of India conquered by 1856 closes the Company's expansion that 31562 explains by its superior weapons. 31566 begins with the sparks of revolt that follow.
Pay, mansions, servants, a pittance and slow promotions are the three sepoys' complaints listed in 31570.
The greased cartridge told to the Brahmin sepoys is the spark itself, which this set holds as 31566. 31570 is the pay-and-promotion grievance, a standing complaint rather than the trigger.

Who the masses sheltered belongs to the revolt the popular leaders of 31567 roused the people for. NOTE: the marked key is 'Englishmen'; the comic says the masses helped the patriots, so the key looks wrong.
The sepoys marching on Delhi is the outbreak that 31566 asks learners to locate. 31567 is who led the revolt once it had started.
Losing land under the new land rules is the peasants' side of the ruin, which this set carries as the farmer-and-tax-officer exchange, 31569. 31564 is the artisans.
Kunwar Singh is one of the revolt's leaders, and 31567 is where the set holds them. 31561 is the earlier generation of princes.
Offering the shot wrist to Mother Ganga is the same Kunwar Singh panel, so it sits with the leaders of the revolt, 31567.
